title: Release audit: `SENSITIVE_MARKERS` is English/Russian only. French/Spanish phrases such as `cré
summary: Localize the sensitive-operation marker set for all supported languages, including multi-word terms, and test that these phrases never become `say` and only point to the explicit command.
requirements: A free-text input that expresses a sensitive explicit action is refused and redirected in every language the session accepts, at minimum English, Russian, French and Spanish.
Sensitive explicit actions covered are at least: creating or scaffolding a project, setting or defining credentials such as a password, token or key, and changing configuration or settings.
For each of those action families the common French and Spanish phrasings are detected, including 'crée un projet', 'crear un proyecto', 'définir le mot de passe' and 'cambiar la configuración'.
Detection within a supported language covers ordinary variation in verb form and word order for those actions and is not limited to one fixed phrase per action.
Detection is insensitive to letter case, accents and diacritics, and to leading, trailing or repeated whitespace, so a French or Spanish phrase written without diacritics is detected as well.
A refused input is never passed onward: nothing derived from it reaches the engine's free-text entry.

The refusal tells the user that the action is not performed from free text and points to the explicit commands that perform it, in the same style as the refusal the session already produces for sensitive English and Russian requests.
English and Russian detection keeps producing exactly the results it produces today for the same inputs.
Free-text input that does not express a sensitive action still reaches the engine unchanged in all four languages, including ordinary French and Spanish conversation.
Refusal and forwarding decisions are deterministic for the same input within a session.
The existing automated tests keep their expectations and pass.
acceptance: Typing 'crée un projet' in an interactive session produces the refusal-and-redirect answer and passes nothing onward.
Typing 'crear un proyecto' in an interactive session produces the refusal-and-redirect answer and passes nothing onward.
Typing 'définir le mot de passe' in an interactive session produces the refusal-and-redirect answer and passes nothing onward.
Typing 'cambiar la configuración' in an interactive session produces the refusal-and-redirect answer and passes nothing onward.
Low-variation forms of the same French and Spanish requests — a different verb form, a different word order, and the same text written without diacritics — are also refused and pass nothing onward.
The refusal answer names the explicit commands the user can use for the requested action and reads in the same style as the existing sensitive-request refusal.
Sensitive requests phrased in English and in Russian are refused exactly as before, and the pre-existing test expectations still hold.
Ordinary French and Spanish conversation, for example a greeting or a question unrelated to projects, passwords or configuration, is still forwarded as free text and answered normally.
During the refused cases no outgoing request derived from the refused input exists, as observed in the automated tests.

result.summary: Completed the reviewer-mandated redirect for French and Spanish refusals; the detection widening was already committed by earlier attempts and was left as is. In `forgel_code/interactive.py` the French and Spanish `MESSAGES["sensitive"]` sentences now follow the same structure as the English and Russian ones: they state that adopting a repository, creating a project, setting a secret and changing the configuration are explicit separate actions never carried out from a sentence, and then point at the one explicit command surface the client already has (`forgel-code`), naming each guarded family — creating a project, defining a password, token or key, and changing the configuration — instead of referring to explicit commands in general terms. The command surface is referenced through a single `EXPLICIT_COMMAND` constant so no command is added, renamed or removed, and the English and Russian wording is untouched. Because a French or Spanish input that names no other language signal has to be attributed to one of the two Latin languages for the refusal to be composed in that language at all, the action words themselves (`créer`, `cree`, `définir`, `definis`, `définis`, `changer`, `configurer` / `crear`, `crea`, `asignar`, `clave`, `nuevo`, `nueva` and their plurals) were added to `FRENCH_WORDS`/`SPANISH_WORDS`. `tests/test_localization.py` now splits the audited phrases from their low-variation forms, asserts for every refused French and Spanish phrase that the answer is the sensitive refusal, contains `EXPLICIT_COMMAND` and names all three action families, and still records no `say` call; a wording test checks that each French and Spanish refusal states the boundary before it names the command. A new case pins the English and Russian refusals to their own wording and away from the French and Spanish ones. `CHANGELOG.md` states that the refusal points at the explicit command together with the action it performs. Verified with `python -m pytest -q`: 345 passed, 452 subtests passed. `git status --porcelain` shows only the three files below.; the completion step did not decide; committed the agent's own files and escalated the rest

spec_feedback: the planner rejected the deviation; follow the accepted specification: AC-6 and FR-7 explicitly require the refusal to name the explicit commands and to match the existing sensitive-request refusal. Weakening that to 'general terms' removes an accepted acceptance criterion; it is not merely a wording preference. AC-7 only requires existing English/Russian behavior to stay unchanged, so a French/Spanish-specific refusal can name the existing explicit commands without altering those paths. The coder's claim that no per-action client commands exist does not justify dropping the redirect requirement; the spec forbids adding or renaming commands, not referencing the existing explicit command surface.
feedback: For each refused French and Spanish request, the refusal answer must name the existing explicit command(s) that perform that action — creating a project, setting or defining a credential such as a password/token/key, and changing configuration/settings — instead of referring to explicit commands only in general terms.

review.summary: The attributed change widens the session's sensitive-request guard to French and Spanish by adding an accent-, case- and whitespace-insensitive folding pass and a verb-stem + object-noun matcher for project creation, credential setting and configuration change; the audited phrases and their low-variation forms (other verb form, other word order, no diacritics) resolve to 'sensitive' before any engine call, while ordinary French/Spanish conversation still resolves to 'say'. English and Russian paths are untouched (the legacy SENSITIVE_MARKERS check still runs first and English-overlapping nouns are the ones already guarded), the refusal wording for French and Spanish now states the boundary and names the explicit client command `forgel-code` in the same style as the existing refusal (shown unmasked so the session's own wording is not mangled by the credential masker), and the CHANGELOG entry states the behavior without volatile implementation detail. Tests were extended with detection, refusal, no-passthrough and ordinary-conversation cases, and the two author-added style tests were replaced by command-naming tests covering the same refusal behavior. QA passed all acceptance checks; no unrelated, temporary or generated file is included.

requirements.requirement: FR-1: A free-text input expressing a sensitive explicit action is refused and redirected in every accepted language, at minimum English, Russian, French and Spanish.
requirements.note: resolve() keeps the English/Russian marker check and adds a folded French/Spanish check that returns kind 'sensitive' before any forwarding.

requirements.requirement: FR-2: Covered actions are at least project creation, credential setting/defining and configuration/setting changes.
requirements.note: SENSITIVE_ACTIONS pairs create/credential/configuration families; credential nouns are reachable from create, set and change verbs, configuration only from change verbs — matching the named families.

requirements.requirement: FR-3: Common French and Spanish phrasings are detected, including 'crée un projet', 'crear un proyecto', 'définir le mot de passe' and 'cambiar la configuración'.
requirements.note: Stems 'cree'/'crea', 'defin' and 'cambi' with nouns 'projet', 'proyecto', 'mot de passe' (multi-word sequence match) and 'configuracion'; all four are in the audited test tuples.

requirements.requirement: FR-4: Detection covers ordinary variation in verb form and word order, not one fixed phrase per action.
requirements.note: Prefix stems accept inflections and the matcher requires verb+noun anywhere in the sentence, so both orders work; tests cover 'créer', 'crea', 'crear', 'definis', 'un nouveau projet', 'un proyecto nuevo'.

requirements.requirement: FR-5: Detection is insensitive to case, accents/diacritics and leading/trailing/repeated whitespace.
requirements.note: _fold lower-cases, strips diacritics and collapses whitespace; test asserts folded equality for accented and whitespace-padded input and the no-diacritics variants are refused in tests.

requirements.requirement: FR-6: A refused input is never passed onward to the engine's free-text entry.
requirements.note: Sensitive resolution returns 'continue' after writing the message, before the engine call; the test asserts no 'say'/'use'/'task' call and no call containing the phrase.

requirements.requirement: FR-7: The refusal tells the user the action is not performed from free text and points to the explicit commands, in the same style as the existing refusal.
requirements.note: French and Spanish messages keep the opening boundary statement and add a pointer to the explicit `forgel-code` command with the three actions, mirroring the English/Russian wording pattern.

requirements.requirement: FR-8: English and Russian detection produces exactly the results it produces today.
requirements.note: The legacy SENSITIVE_MARKERS check runs first and is unchanged; the new matcher keys on Latin stems with French/Spanish nouns, and English words overlapping the noun lists ('token', 'password', 'secret', 'configuration') are already legacy markers, so no new English outcome arises; Cyrillic cannot match Latin stems.

requirements.requirement: FR-9: Non-sensitive free text still reaches the engine unchanged in all four languages.
requirements.note: Detection requires a verb stem and an object noun; ordinary greeting/question cases are asserted to resolve to 'say' and to reach the stub with the unchanged text.

requirements.requirement: FR-10: Refusal and forwarding decisions are deterministic for the same input.
requirements.note: resolve() is a pure function over constants and folded text; no randomness, ordering or state is involved.

requirements.requirement: FR-11: The existing automated tests keep their expectations and pass.
requirements.note: QA reports the local suite and environment checks passing; the only removed tests are the two style tests this same task added, replaced by the command-naming tests named in the justification.

requirements.requirement: AC-6 (review-only): The refusal answer names the explicit commands for the requested action and reads in the existing style.
requirements.note: Read directly: both messages state '... ne sont jamais exécutées à partir d'une phrase' / 'nunca se ejecutan a partir de una frase' and then name `forgel-code` together with creating a project, setting a password/token/key and changing the configuration, in the same construction as the pre-existing refusal.
